newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican markets rocked by 'decertification' fears.
newsitem.headline: Mexican markets rocked by 'decertification' fears.

text.p: The peso plunged sharply on Thursday as Mexico's finance minister warned that a potential U.S. decision to decertify Mexico as an ally in the war on drugs could damage the economy.

U.S. law requires the annual certification to Congress by the president of whether Mexico and 31 other countries are partners in the international battle against drug trafficking. Countries that fail the test face possible economic sanctions. A decision is due by Saturday.
"Of course it (decertification) would affect the cooperation in the fight against drug trafficking, and this is not good for the economy and nor is it good for the markets," Ortiz told reporters.
Mexican financial markets went into a tailspin on Thursday, fuelled in part by concerns over potential decertification, traders and analysts said.

The Mexican peso lost 2.21 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar, falling 17.6 centavos to 7.98 pesos per dollar on the benchmark 48-hour contract. It was the largest one-day fall since a drop of 3.34 percent on Nov. 14, 1995, when Mexico was in the midst of an economic crisis.
The Mexican stock market fell by 1.04 percent on Thursday, and prices tumbled on the secondary money market.

"I don't believe the effects will be very strong in the short term if the certification is not given, but certainly the environment of cooperation favours economic activity and the markets," Ortiz said.

The certification process is widely reviled in Mexico as a case of U.S. meddling in Mexican affairs. Mexican congressmen on Wednesday blasted Washington for grading other countries' anti-drug efforts while the demand for narcotics is so high in the United States.

Mexico has passed the annual test since 1986, but a series of embarrassing recent events in Mexico has led many Democratic senators and congressmen to urge President Bill Clinton to deny certification this year.
Last week Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, former chief of the country's anti-drug efforts, was arrested on charges that he was in the employ of one of the country's top drug lords.
In addition, a series of stories in The New York Times, citing U.S. officials and reports, has alleged that many current and former Mexican officials had intimate ties with major drug traffickers.
Most of the illicit cocaine headed to the United States is funnelled through Mexico, where traffickers spend billions of dollars a year bribing local officials in exchange for safe passage.
